title: fighting slop with slop — Vaibhav Gupta, Boundary
talk_summary: A talk from Boundary (BAML) arguing that since agents write most code, teams should stop relying on human code review and instead encode invariants into tooling: a tiny architecture.md, design-doc workflows with read-requirements, dependency-graph CI checks, and agent-driven transcript analysis of tool-call efficiency. The concrete, copyable parts are the small invariant files, the agent-inspects-agent-transcripts loop, and AB-testing of agent-facing interfaces by tool-call count and error rate.

takeaways.technique: Tiny invariant architecture file instead of per-model prompt files
takeaways.what_they_do: Maintain one very small architecture.md (not Claude.md) containing only things stable for months/years, e.g. compiler layers, so any model can consume it regardless of vendor.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We built an architecture.md file. Instead of using Claude.md, just pick something that every model can just understand. This file has to be incredibly small

takeaways.technique: Agents inspect other agents' execution transcripts for inefficiency
takeaways.what_they_do: Run agents on fresh tasks, capture the full transcript (tools used, steps taken), then have a second agent find not just correctness bugs but wasted tool calls ('what took three tool calls when it should have only taken one'), with humans triaging real vs hallucinated findings.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we can have agents go inspect them. And agents find what was good, what was bad... what took three tool calls when it should have only taken one

takeaways.technique: AB-test agent-facing interfaces by tool-call count and error rate
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of guessing which tool/API shape is better for agents, run both variants and deterministically compare tool calls, errors, and correct outcomes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you could go and AB test it. You could figure out which ones took less tool calls, which one took uh which one made less errors

takeaways.what_they_do: Build a dependency-graph tool with semantic package boundaries and CLI checks that fail CI when an agent adds a leaky dependency or breaks an invariant, so architecture converges without human review.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we can go build CLI tools that guarantee that certain invariants can't be broken... we now have CI/CD changing or a simple Git commit history that tells us exactly where things break

takeaways.technique: Design-doc workflow with mandatory readership before shipping
takeaways.what_they_do: Design docs live as markdown + CLI (GitHub-like without GitHub) with versioning/commenting and a Slack channel that notifies on updates; a rule requires people to actually read a doc before it ships, which curbed doc spam and raised quality.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you're going to ship a design doc, you require people to actually go read it. And with this last standard, we suddenly had design docs that were incredibly high quality

takeaways.technique: Replace line-reading review with execution traces and semantic navigation
takeaways.what_they_do: Argue that when nobody reads all code, understanding must come from execution traces and semantic-boundary navigation (expand/collapse packages, jump to exact lines) rather than full diffs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: in a world where we don't read all the code, the only way to understand the code is actually by the execution trace
